title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Method
Tolerance limits are different from confidence intervals in that they provide an interval within which at least a proportion \(q\) of the population lies, within probability \(1-\alpha\) or more that the stated interval does indeed “contain” the proportion \(q\) of the population.
With a sample size of \(n\), there is a probability that at least \(1-\alpha\) that at least \(q\) [or \((100)(q)%\)] of the population is between \(X^{(r)}\) and \(X^{(n+1-m)}\) inclusive. For one-sided tolerance regions let either \(r\) or \(m = 0\), where \(X^{(r)}\) and \(X^{(n+1)}\) are considered to be \(-\infty\) and \(+\infty\) respectively, and then proceed with methods.

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Data
The data consists of a random sample \(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n\) from a larger population. A confidence coefficient is chosen, \(1-\alpha\) and a pair of integers \(r\) and \(m\) are chosen as well.
Important Note! We try to make the statement: “The probability is \(1-\alpha\) that the random interval from \(X^{(r)}\) to \(X^{(n+1-m)}\) inclusive contains a proportion \(q\) or more of the population.”

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Assumptions

The \(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n\) are a random sample.
The measurement scale is at least ordinal.

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Approach
Approach A (to find \(n\)):

Used when we want to determine the required sample size \(n\) after selecting a desired population proportion \(q\)
If \(r+m = 1\), or if either \(r\) or \(m = 0\) as a one-sided tolerance limit, read \(n\) directly from Table A5 to find the appropriate values of \(\alpha\) and \(q\).
If \(r+m=2\), read \(n\) from Table A6 for the appropriate values of \(\alpha\) and \(q\).
If Table A5 and A6 are not appropriate, use the approximation:

\[
n \cong \frac 14 x_{1-\alpha} \frac {1+q} {1-q} + \frac 12 (r+m-1)
\] where \(x_{1-\alpha}\) is the \((1-\alpha)\) quantile of a chi-squared random variable with \(2(r+m)\) degrees of freedom, obtained from Table A2.
Approach B (to find \(q\)):

Used when we want to determine the population proportion \(q\) for a given sample size \(n\)
For a given sample size \(n\) and selected values of \(\alpha\), \(r\), and \(m\), the approximate value of \(q\), the proportion of the population, is given by:

\[
q = \frac {4n-2(r+m-1)-x_{1-\alpha}} {4n-2(r+m-1)+x_{1-\alpha}}
\]

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Completed Homework Problem

A fitness gym has measured the percentage of fat on 86 of its members.


At least what percent of its members have fat percentage between the smallest and largest of the percentages measured on the 86 members of the sample, with 95% certainty? With 90% certainty?
At least what percent of its members have fat percentage between \(X^{(2)}\) and \(X^{(85)}\) with 95% certainty? With 90% certainty?

Part a:

# part (a): [X(1), X(86)]
p95 <- 1 - 0.05^(1/86)
p90 <- 1 - 0.10^(1/86)

p95

[1] 0.03423437

p90

[1] 0.02641899


With 95% confidence, we can say at least 3.42% of the population lies between the smallest and largest observed fat percentages. With 90% confidence, we can say at least 2.64% of the population lies between the smallest and largest observed fat percentages.
Part b:

# part (b): [X(2), X(85)]
p95 <- qbeta(0.05, 84, 3)
p90 <- qbeta(0.10, 84, 3)

p95

[1] 0.9286002

p90

[1] 0.9392982


With 95% confidence, at least 92.86% of the population have fat percentage between \(X^{(2)}\) and \(X^{(85)}\). With 90% confidence, at least 93.93% of the population have fat percentage between \(X^{(2)}\) and \(X^{(85)}\).

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Method
The sign test is the more simple version of the binomial test with \(p^* = 1/2 = 1 - p^*\). The sign test is useful when trying to find out whether one random variable in a pair \((X, Y)\) is larger than the other random variable in the pair. The data will consist of observations on a bivariate random sample \((X_1, Y_1), (X_2, Y_2), ... , (X_n, Y_n)\) where there are \(n'\) pairs of observations. With each pair, a comparison is made, and the comparison is then classified as either “+” (plus, if \(X_i < Y_i\)) or “-” (minus, if \(X_i > Y_i\)) or “0” (tie, if \(X_i = Y_i\)).

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Assumptions

The bivariate random variables \((X_i, Y_i), i = 1, 2, ..., n'\) are mutually independent.
The measurement scale is at least ordinal within each pair (i.e. each can be classified as plus, minus, or tie).
Pairs are internally consistent (i.e. if \(P(+) > P(-)\) for one pair, it is for all pairs).

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)

The Wilcoxon signed rank test is the parametric equivalent if we assume the difference \(Y_i - X_i\) are random variables with a symmetric distribution function (i.e. the distribution function of a random variable \(Z\) is symmetric about some point \(c\) if \(P(Z \leq c - x) = P(Z \geq c + x)\) for all \(x\)).
The paired \(t\)-test is the parametric equivalent if the differences \(Y_i - X_i\) are independent and identically distributed normal random variables.

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Hypotheses

\(H_0\): \(P(+) = P(-)\) (two-tailed) | \(P(+) \geq P(-)\) (left-tailed) | \(P(+) \leq P(-)\) (right-tailed)
\(H_A\): \(P(+) \neq P(-)\) (two-tailed) | \(P(+) < P(-)\) (left-tailed) | \(P(+) > P(-)\) (right-tailed)

In terms of null distribution, it could be interpreted in the following ways:

Two-tailed:

\(H_0\): \(E(X_i) = E(Y_i)\) for all i (for means) | \(M\) of \(X_i = M\) of \(Y_i\) for all i (for medians)
\(H_A\): \(E(X_i) \neq E(Y_i)\) for all i | \(M\) of \(X_i \neq M\) of \(Y_i\) for all i

Left-tailed:

\(H_0\): \(E(X_i) \leq E(Y_i)\) for all i (for means) | \(M\) of \(X_i \leq M\) of \(Y_i\) for all i (for medians)
\(H_A\): \(E(X_i) > E(Y_i)\) for all i | \(M\) of \(X_i > M\) of \(Y_i\) for all i

Right-tailed:

\(H_0\): \(E(X_i) \geq E(Y_i)\) for all i (for means) | \(M\) of \(X_i \geq M\) of \(Y_i\) for all i (for medians)
\(H_A\): \(E(X_i) < E(Y_i)\) for all i | \(M\) of \(X_i < M\) of \(Y_i\) for all i

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Rejection Region
Two-tailed:

For \(n \leq 20\), use Table A3 with \(n\) and \(p=1/2\); find about \(\alpha/2\) and call it \(\alpha_1\). The value of \(y\) corresponding to \(\alpha_1\) is \(t\).
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T \leq t\) or if \(T \geq n - t\) at a level of significance of \(2\alpha_1\)
For \(n > 20\), use the normal approximation to get: \[
t = \frac{1}{2} (n + z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{n})
\] where \(z_{\alpha/2}\) is obtained from Table A1. And, if \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(z_{\alpha/2} = (-1.96)\), then: \[
t = \frac{n}{2} - \sqrt{n}
\]

Left-tailed:

Note: small values of \(T\) indicate that a minus is more probable than a plus (agreeing with \(H_1\))
For \(n \leq 20\), use Table A3 with \(n\) and \(p=1/2\); find about \(\alpha\) and call it \(\alpha_1\). The value of \(y\) corresponding to \(\alpha_1\) is \(t\).
For \(n > 20\), \(t\) is found using this approximation: \[
t = \frac{1}{2} (n + z_{\alpha} \sqrt{n})
\]
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T \leq t\) at a significance level of \(\alpha_1\) or \(\alpha\).

Right-tailed:

Note: big values of \(T\) indicate that a plus is more probable than a minus (agreeing with \(H_1\))
For \(n \leq 20\), use Table A3 with \(n\) and \(p=1/2\); find about \(\alpha\) and call it \(\alpha_1\). The value of \(y\) corresponding to \(\alpha_1\) is \(t\). (same as left-tailed test)
For \(n > 20\), \(t\) is found using the same approximation as the left-tailed test.

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: \(T\) is the number of “plus” pairs (i.e. \(T=\) number of pairs \((X_i, Y_i)\) where \(X_i < Y_i\)).
The null distribution of \(T\) is the binomial distribution with \(p = 1/2\) and \(n=\) number of noted pairs (i.e. disregard all tied pairs \(X=Y\) and let \(n=\) total number of pluses and minuses). Normal approximation is used for \(n>20\).
The p-value is obtained differently for the different forms:

Two-tailed: p-value is twice the smaller of the probabilities that \(Y \leq\) or \(\geq\) the observed value of \(T\) (found from Table A3 for \(n \leq 20\), Table A1 if \(n > 20\))
Left-tailed: p-value is the probability that \(Y \leq\) observed value of \(T\)
Right-tailed: p-value is the probability that \(Y \geq\) observed value of \(T\)

text:
Completed Homework Problem

Six students went on a diet in an attempt to lose weight, with the following results: (given in code below). Is the diet an effective means of losing weight?


#create a data set w/ the paired data given
weight_before <- c(174, 191, 188, 182, 201, 188)
weight_after <- c(165, 186, 183, 178, 203, 181)

sign.test(x=weight_before, y=weight_after, alternative="less")

$n
[1] 6

$alternative
[1] "less"

$T
[1] 1

$p.value
[1] 0.109375


Hypotheses

\(H_0:\) \(P(+) \geq P(-)\), where \(P(+) = P\)(weight_before < weight_after) and \(P(-) = P\)(weight_before > weight_after)
\(H_1:\) \(P(+) < P(-)\)

Test Statistic and p-Value

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Method
The McNemar test aims to answer the question: “Can we detect a difference between the probability of (0,1) and the probability of (1,0)?” This is a different version of the sign test where the data is on a nominal measurement scale with categories “0” and “1”. The data will consist of observations on \(n'\) independent bivariate random variables \((X_i, Y_i), i = 1, 2, ..., n'\).
The data is usually organized into a contingency table, where \(a\) = the number of pairs where \(X_i = 0\) and \(Y_i = 0\); \(b\) = the number of pairs where \(X_i = 0\) and \(Y_i = 1\); \(c\) = the number of pairs where \(X_i = 1\) and \(Y_i = 0\); and \(d\) = the number of pairs where \(X_i = 1\) and \(Y_i = 1\).

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Assumptions

The pairs \((X_i, Y_i)\) are mutually independent.
The measurement scale is nominal with two categories “0” and “1” for all \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\)
The difference \(P(X_i = 0, Y_i = 1) - P(X_i = 1, Y_i = 0)\) is negative/zero/positive for all \(i\)

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
The McNemar test is equivalent to the paired sample t-tests but for dichotomous dependent variables, as opposed to for continuous dependent variables by the paired sample tests (via https://real-statistics.com/non-parametric-tests/mcnemars-test/).

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Hypotheses

\(H_0\): \(P(X_i = 0, Y_i = 1) = P(X_i = 1, Y_i = 0)\) for all \(i\)
\(H_A\): \(P(X_i = 0, Y_i = 1) \neq P(X_i = 1, Y_i = 0)\) for all \(i\)

These hypotheses can also be interpreted like this, if we add \(P(X_i = 0, Y_i = 0)\) to both sides:

\(H_0\): \(P(X_i = 0) = P(Y_i = 0)\) for all \(i\) | \(P(X_i = 1) = P(Y_i = 1)\) for all \(i\)
\(H_A\): \(P(X_i = 0) \neq P(Y_i = 0)\) for all \(i\) | \(P(X_i = 1) \neq P(Y_i = 1)\) for all \(i\)

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Rejection Region

Let \(n=b+c\). If \(n \leq 20\), use Table A3. Enter table with \(p=1/2\) and \(n=b+c\) to find approximately \(\alpha/2\) (called \(\alpha_1\)). The corresponding value of \(y\) is \(t\). Reject \(H_0\) if \(T_2 \leq t\) or if \(T_2 \geq n - t\) at a significance level of \(2\alpha_1\).
If \(n>20\), use \(T_1\) and Table A2. Reject \(H_0\) at a level of significance \(\alpha\) if \(T_1\) exceeds the \((1-\alpha)\) quantile of a chi-squared random variable with 1 degree of freedom.

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic:

For \(b+c > 20\): \(T_1 = \frac{(b-c)^2}{b+c}\)
For \(b+c \leq 20\): \(T_2 = b\)

The null distribution of \(T_1\) is approximately the chi-squared distribution with 1 degree of freedom when \((b+c)\) is large. The exact distribution of \(T_2\) is the binomial distribution with \(p=1/2\) and \(n=b+c\).
For \(n \leq 20\), the p-value is twice the probability of \(T_2 \leq\) \(\geq\) the observed value (whichever is smaller). For \(n>20\), the p-value is the probability of \(T_1\) exceeding the observed value (as found in Table A2 for the chi-squared distribution with 1 degree of freedom).

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
R function
R function for McNemar test (obtained from https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/mcnemar.test)
mcnemar.test(x, y = NULL, correct = TRUE)
where x is either a two-dimensional contingency table in matrix form or a factor object, y is a factor object (it will be ignored if x is a matrix), and correct indicates whether or not to apply continuity correction when computing the test statistic.

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Completed Homework Problem

One hundred thirty-five citizens were selected at random and were asked to state their opinion regarding the U.S. foreign policy. Forty-three were opposed to the U.S. foreign policy. After several weeks, during which they received an informative newsletter, they were again asked their opinion, 37 were opposed, and 30 of the 37 were persons who originally were not opposed to the U.S. foreign policy. Is the change in numbers of people opposed to the U.S. foreign policy significant?

Corresponding contingency table: | Before  After | Opposed | Not Opposed | |—————-|———|————-| | Opposed | 7 | 36 | | Not Opposed | 30 | 62 |
From this table, let’s make a matrix of these values to enter into the McNemar test function.

foreign_policy <- matrix(c(7, 36,
                           30, 62),
                         nrow = 2,
                         byrow = TRUE)

mcnemar.test(foreign_policy, correct = TRUE)


    McNemar's Chi-squared test with continuity correction

data:  foreign_policy
McNemar's chi-squared = 0.37879, df = 1, p-value = 0.5383


Hypotheses

\(H_0\): \(P(X_i = 0, Y_i = 1) = P(X_i = 1, Y_i = 0)\) for all \(i\)
\(H_A\): \(P(X_i = 0, Y_i = 1) \neq P(X_i = 1, Y_i = 0)\) for all \(i\)

where \(X_i\) represents the before opposed for person \(i\) (“1” = opposed, “0” = not opposed), and \(Y_i\) represents after opposed for person \(i\) (“1” = opposed, “0” = not opposed).
Test Statistic and p-Value

\(\chi^2 = 0.37879\)
\(p = 0.5383\)

Rejection Region

Reject \(H_0\) if \(p < \alpha\); \(\alpha=0.05\).

Conclusion/Interpretation

Fail to reject \(H_0\).
There is not sufficient evidence to suggest that the change in numbers of people opposed to the U.S. foreign policy is significant.

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Method
The Cox and Stuart test for trend involves pairing the later numbers with the earlier numbers and performing a sign test on the pairs. A trend is present if one member of each pair has a tendency to be higher/lower than the other member. A trend is not present if the sequence of numbers actually represents observations on independent and identically distributed random variables (i.e. no tendency for one member to exceed the other one). It can also be used to detect any specified type of nonrandom pattern (i.e. sine wave, periodic pattern).
NOTE: A sequence of numbers is said to have a trend if the later numbers in the sequence tend to be greater than the earlier numbers (upward trend) or less than the earlier numbers (downward trend).
The data will consist of observations on a sequence of random variables \(X_1, X_2, ..., X_{n'}\), arranged in a particular order. Group the random variables into pairs \((X_1, X_{1+c}), (X_2, X_{2+c}), ..., (X_{n'-c}, X_{n'})\), where \(c = n'/2\) if \(n'\) is even, otherwise \(c=(n'+1)/2\). Replace each pair \((X_i, X_{i+c})\) with a “+” if \(X_i < X_{i+c}\) or a “-” if \(X_i > X_{i+c}\). Eliminate ties. The number of untied pairs is called \(n\).

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Assumptions

The random variables \(X_1, X_2, ..., X_{n'}\) are mutually independent
The measurement scale of the \(X_i\)s is at least ordinal
Either the \(X_i\)s are identically distributed or there is a trend; meaning that the random variables are more likely to be greater than instead of less than the earlier random variables (or vice versa).

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
There is no direct parametric equivalent that I am able to find.

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Hypotheses
The hypotheses are the same as the sign test. The null hypothesis is that no trend is present. A right-tailed test is used to detect an upward trend, and a left-tailed test is used to detect a downward trend. The two-tailed test is used if the alternative hypothesis is that any type of trend (upward or downward) exists.

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Rejection Region
The rejection region is the same as the sign test.

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: \(T\) = total number of +’s
The null distribution of \(T\) is approximately the binomial distribution with \(p=1/2\) and \(n=\) number of untied pairs, where \(X_i \neq X_{i+c}\).
The p-value is calculated exactly as in the sign test.

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
R function
R function for Cox-Stuart test (obtained from https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/randtests/versions/1.0.1/topics/cox.stuart.test)

##load in library first
library(randtests)

cox.stuart.test(x, alternative)
where x is a numeric vector containing the data, and alternative is the alternative hypothesis (“two.sided” is default, can also use “left.sided” or “right.sided”).

title: Week 04: Chapter 3.3-3.5
text:
Completed Homework Problem

In a certain city the mortality rate per 100,000 citizens due to automobile accidents for each of the last 15 years was (see below). Is there any basis for the statement that the mortality rate is increasing?


mortality_rate <- c(17.3, 17.9, 18.4, 18.1, 18.3, 19.6, 18.6, 19.2, 17.7, 20.0, 19.0, 18.8, 19.3, 20.2, 19.9)
cox.stuart.test(mortality_rate, "right.sided")


    Cox Stuart test

data:  mortality_rate
statistic = 7, n = 7, p-value = 0.007812
alternative hypothesis: increasing trend


Hypotheses

\(H_0:\) no trend is present
\(H_1:\) an upward/increasing trend is present

Test Statistic and p-Value

\(T = 7\)
\(p = 0.007812\)

Rejection Region

Reject \(H_0\) if \(p < \alpha\); \(\alpha=0.05\).

Conclusion/Interpretation

Reject \(H_0\).
There is sufficient evidence to suggest that the mortality rate is increasing.

title: Week 07: Chapter 5.1-5.2
text:
Method
The Mann-Whitney test is also known as the Wilcoxon ranked sum test. It is used to compare two independent random samples. Let \(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n\) denote the random sample of size \(n\) from population 1. Let \(Y_1, Y_2, ..., Y_m\) denote the random sample of size \(m\) from population 2. Assign the ranks 1 to \(n+m\) to the observations from smallest to largest. Let \(R(X_i)\) and \(R(Y_j)\) be the rank assigned to \(X_i\) and \(Y_j\) for all \(i\) and \(j\). Note: \(N = n+m\). If several sample values are exactly equal to each other (tied) assign to each the average of the ranks that would have been assigned to them had there been no ties.

title: Week 07: Chapter 5.1-5.2
text:
Assumptions

Both samples are random samples from their respective populations.
In addition to independence within each sample, there is mutual independence between the two samples
The measurement scale is at least ordinal

title: Week 07: Chapter 5.1-5.2
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
The parametric equivalent of the Mann-Whitney test is the independent samples t-test. It is used to measure the differences/compare means of two independent samples. More can be found here: https://libguides.library.kent.edu/spss/independentttest

title: Week 07: Chapter 5.1-5.2
text:
Hypotheses
Two-tailed:

\(H_0\): \(F(x) = G(x)\) for all \(x\)
\(H_A\): \(F(x) \neq G(x)\) for some \(x\) OR \(P(X > Y) \neq P(X<Y)\)

Left-tailed:

\(H_0\): \(F(x) = G(x)\) for all \(x\)
\(H_A\): \(F(x) > G(x)\) for some \(x\) OR \(E(X) < E(Y)\) OR \(P(X > Y) < P(X<Y)\)

Right-tailed:

\(H_0\): \(F(x) = G(x)\) for all \(x\)
\(H_A\): \(F(x) < G(x)\) for some \(x\) OR \(E(X) > E(Y)\) OR \(P(X > Y) > P(X<Y)\)

where \(F(x)\) and \(G(x)\) are the distribution functions corresponding to \(X\) and \(Y\) respectively. ## Rejection Region Two-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at a level of significance \(\alpha\) if \(T\) is less than its \(\alpha/2\) quantile or greater than its \(1-\alpha/2\) quantile obtained from Table A7 for \(n \leq 20\) and \(m \leq 20\). Otherwise obtained from table A1 (even in the case of \(T_1\))

Left-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at a level of significance \(\alpha\) if \(T\) is less than its \(\alpha/2\) quantile or greater than its \(1-\alpha/2\) quantile obtained from Table A7 for \(n \leq 20\) and \(m \leq 20\). If \(T_1\) is used, reject \(H_0\) if \(T_1 < z_\alpha\)

Right-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at a level of significance \(\alpha\) if \(T\) is less than its \(\alpha/2\) quantile or greater than its \(1-\alpha/2\) quantile obtained from Table A7 for \(n \leq 20\) and \(m \leq 20\). If \(T_1\) is used, reject \(H_0\) if \(T_1 > z_{\alpha-1}\)

title: Week 07: Chapter 5.1-5.2
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: If there are no/few ties, the sum of the ranks assigned to the sample from population 1 can be used as a test statistic. \[
T = \sum_{i=1}^n R(X_i)
\] If there are many ties, subtract the mean from \(T\) and divide by the standard deviation to get:

\[
T_1 = \frac{T-n \frac{N+1}{2}}{\sqrt{\frac{nm}{N(N-1)}  \sum_{i=1}^N R_i^2- \frac{nm(N+1)^2}{4(N-1)}}}
\] where \(\sum R_i^2\) refers to the sum of the squares of all \(N\) of the ranks or average ranks actually used in both samples.

The approximate quantiles are found using the normal approximation in the case of no ties, and \(n\) or \(m>20\). If there are many ties, then \(T_1\) is used instead of \(T\) and \(T_1\) is approximately a standard normal random variable whose quanitles are given in Table A1.
The p-value is obtained differently for each different tailed test:

Two-tailed: In the case of \(T\), substitute \(T\) or \(T'\) into the following equation:


\[
2*P(Z \leq \frac{T+ \frac{1}{2} - n \frac{N+1}{2}}{\sqrt{\frac{nm(N+1)}{12}}})
\] where \(Z\) is a standard normal random variable. In the case of \(T_1\), the p-value is twice the smaller of \(P(Z \ leq T_1)\) or \(P(Z \geq T_1)\) - Left-tailed: similarly to the equation above, but without multiplying it by 2. In the case of \(T_1\) the p-value is approximately \(P(Z \leq T_1\) obtained from Table A1. - Right-tailed: similarly to the equation above, but without multiplying it by 2. If \(T_1\) is used, p-value = \(P(Z \geq T_1) = 1-P(Z \leq T_1)\) obtained from Table A1.

text: Confidence Interval

title: Week 07: Chapter 5.1-5.2
text:
Data
The data consists of two random samples \(X_1, ..., X_n\) and \(Y_1,...,Y_m\) of size \(n\) and \(m\). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) denote random variables with the same distribution as the two random samples.

title: Week 07: Chapter 5.1-5.2
text:
Assumptions

Both samples are random samples from their respective populations
Independence within each sample, and mutual independence between the two samples
The two population distribution functions are identical except for a possible difference in location parameters. I.e. there is a constant \(d\) such that \(X\) has the same distribution function as \(Y+d\).

title: Week 07: Chapter 5.1-5.2
text:
Method
Find the \(\alpha/2\) quantile \(w_{\alpha/2}\) for \(n\) and \(m\) from Table A7 if \(n\) and \(m\) are large, where \((1-\alpha)\) is the confidence coefficient. Then calculate \(k\) using: \[
k = w_{\alpha/2} - n(n+1)/2
\] From all the possible pairs \((X_i, Y_j)\) find the \(k\) largest differences \(X_i-Y_j\) and the smallest differences. Ordering each sample from smallest to largest first is convenient, then form a matrix of differences using Xs as rows and Ys as columns. The largest difference is the upper limit \(U\) and the smallest difference is the lower limit \(L\). Then the confidence interval is: \[
P[L \leq E(X) - E(Y) \leq U] \geq 1-\alpha
\]

\(H_A\): at least one \(M_i\) is different

text:
Rejection Region
Reject \(H_0\) if \(\chi_0^2\) is greater than its \(1-\alpha\) quantile from the null distribution.

title: Week 07: Chapter 5.1-5.2
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: Let \(p_j^*\) be the probability of a random observation on \(X\) being in class \(j\), under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true. \[
\chi_0^2 = \frac{12}{n(n+1) \sum_{i =1}^k \frac{R_i^2}{n_i}}-3 (n+1)
\] where \(R_i\) is the sum of the ranks for group \(i\), \(n_i\) is the sample size for group \(i\), \(n = \sum_{i=1}^k n_i\) is the total sample size, and \(k\) is the number of groups.
The chi squared distribution with \(k-1\) degrees of freedom is used as an approximation to the null distribution of \(\chi_0^2\).
The p-value is approximately the probability of chi squared random variable with \(k-1\) degrees of freedom exceeding the observed value of \(\chi_0^2\). \[
p = P[\chi_{k-1}^2 \geq \chi_0^2]
\]

title: Week 08: Chapter 5.3
text:
Method
The Squared ranks test for variances is used to test for equal variances between groups. The data will consist of two random samples. The random samples of \(X_i\)s and \(Y_j\)s must be converted to their absolute deviation from the mean using these two formulas: \[
U_i = |X_i - \mu_1|, i = 1, ..., n
\] \[
V_J = |Y_J - \mu_2|, j = 1, ..., m
\]
where \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are the means from populations 1 and 2. Ranks 1 to \(n +m\) are assigned to the combined sample of Us and Vs. If tied, assign the average of the ranks to each.

title: Week 08: Chapter 5.3
text:
Assumptions

Both samples are random samples from their respective populations
Independence within each sample and mutual independence among the two samples
The measurement scale is at least interval

title: Week 08: Chapter 5.3
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
The parametric equivalent of the squared ranks test for equal variances is the parametric Levene test. I have previously learned the Levene test, and therefore have extensive notes on it already.

title: Week 08: Chapter 5.3
text:
Hypotheses
Two-tailed:

\(H_0\): X and Y are identically distributed, except for possibly different means
\(H_A\): Var(X) \(\neq\) Var(Y)

Left-tailed:

\(H_0\): X and Y are identically distributed, except for possibly different means
\(H_A\): Var(X) < Var(Y)

Right-tailed:

\(H_0\): X and Y are identically distributed, except for possibly different means
\(H_A\): Var(X) > Var(Y)

title: Week 08: Chapter 5.3
text:
Rejection Region
Two-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) if \(T\) is > or < its \(1-\alpha/2\) quantile

Left-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) if \(T\) is < its \(1-\alpha/2\) quantile

Right-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) if \(T\) is > its \(1-\alpha/2\) quantile

title: Week 08: Chapter 5.3
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: If there are no values of \(U\) tied with values of \(V\), the sum of the squares of the ranks assigned to population 1 can be used as the test statistic: \[
T = \sum_{i=1}^n [R(U_i)]^2
\] If there are ties, subtract the mean from \(T\) and divide by standard deviation to get: \[
T_1 = \frac{T-n \overline{R^2}}{[\frac{nm}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i=1}^N R_i^4 - \frac{nm}{N-1} (\overline{R^2})^2]}
\] where \(N = n+m\), \(\overline{R^2}\) represents the average of the squared ranks of both samples combined: \[
\overline{R^2} = \frac{1}{N}  \sum_{i=1}^n [R(U_i)]^2 + \sum_{j=1}^m [R(V_j)]^2
\] and \(\sum R_i^4\) represents the sum of the ranks raised to the 4th power: \[
\sum_{i=1}^N R_i^4 = \sum_{i=1}^n [R(U_i)]^4 + \sum_{j=1}^m [R(V_j)]^4
\]
Quantiles of exact null distribution of \(T\) are in Table A9 for \(n\) and \(m \leq 10\). For \(n\) and \(m > 10\), use the following approximation based on standard normal quantiles \(z_p\) given in Table A_1: \[
w_p = \frac{n(N+1)(2N+1)}{6} + z_p \sqrt{\frac{mn(N+1)(2N+1)(8N+11)}{180}}
\]
The p-value is obtained differently for the different tests:

Two-tailed: p-value = 2*(smaller of the one-tailed p values)
Left-tailed:


\[
P(Z \leq \frac{T-n(N+1)(2N+1)/6}{\sqrt{mn(N+1)(2N+1)(8N+11)/180}})
\]

Right-tailed:

\[
P(Z \geq \frac{T-n(N+1)(2N+1)/6}{\sqrt{mn(N+1)(2N+1)(8N+11)/180}})
\]

title: Week 01-02: Chapters 1-2
text:
Chapter 1 Summary
In chapter 1, we discuss counting rules. I recognized these rules as the rules for combinations, like n choose k. These rules allow us to determine the number of distinguishable arrangements of objects into a row. This can be calculated even if there are one or multiple identical objects present in a group. The total number of possible outcomes of each trial in an experiment can also be determined using counting rules.
Next, we looked at defining and describing experiments and events. We used probabilities to describe events associated with experiments. The probability that an event occurs or does not occur was discussed, along with the probability that an event occurred given that another event occurred, also known as the conditional probability. It was also essential to learn how to identify whether or not two events were independent of each other, which was done by determining if P(AB) = P(A)P(B), where A and B are events.
We then moved onto learning about random variables. Distributions like the discrete uniform distribution and the hypergeometric distribution rely on the probability function of X, where X is a random variable. Distribution functions allow us to view all the properties of a random variable since it shows us all the possible probabilities associated with a random variable. We then use quantiles to describe the overall behavior of a distribution function.
Expected values are used to calculate many different test statistics/statistical values. They are used to calculate the mean, interquartile range (IQR), standard deviation, variance, covariance, and correlation coefficient of random variables.
To conclude chapter 1, the following distributions were defined using probability functions/theorems: normal distribution and chi-squared distribution. Since I have learned and used those distributions in previous courses, I did not focus on this section.

title: Week 01-02: Chapters 1-2
text: Chapter 2 Notes

title: Week 01-02: Chapters 1-2
text:
Chapter 2 Summary
In chapter 2, we shifted focus from counting rules and random variables to sampling, estimation, and hypothesis testing. We began by defining populations and samples. A sample can be random, where each observation is independent and identically distributed, or it can be biased. We also reviewed the following different types of measurement scales: nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio. We saw how order statistics can be applied when analyzing ordered data.
Next, we explored estimation methods. The empirical distribution function (EDF) was introduced as a way to approximate the population distribution based on observed data. We then used concepts like sample mean, variance, and quantiles as point estimators of population parameters. We also learned about interval estimation, confidence coefficients, and unbiased estimators. The bootstrap method was also introduced as a resampling approach to approximate population quantities without requiring prior knowledge of the distribution. In survival analysis, the empirical survival function and the Kaplan-Meier estimator were discussed as nonparametric methods for estimating lifetime distributions.
We then studied hypothesis testing. This included defining null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics, and decision rules. Errors in hypothesis testing were categorized into Type I and Type II errors, with significance level (\(\alpha\)), power, and p-values helping us evaluate tests. We also discussed test properties such as unbiasedness, consistency, and efficiency. We also learned that the power function plays an important role in comparing tests.
Finally, we compared parametric and nonparametric methods. Parametric methods depend on knowing the population distribution. This is unlike nonparametric methods, which are more flexible and robust to distributional assumptions. Nonparametric tests can be applied to nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio data.

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Method
Cramer’s Contingency Coefficient is a way to find the measure of dependence by modifying the \(T\) value (found in previous equations in section 4.3) in a way that the result doesn’t depend as much on the number of degrees of freedom as \(T\) does.
\[
T = \sum_{i = 1}^r  \sum_{j=1}^c   \frac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}
\]

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Approach
Dividing \(T\) by the maximum value \(T\) may attain. Note: large \(T\) values arise from contingency tables with pronounced unevenness among cell counts.
\[
R_1 = \frac{T}{N(q-1)}
\] where \(N\) is the total number of observations, \(q\) is either \(r\) or \(c\) (whichever is smaller) and the maximum value of \(T = N(q-1)\). \(R_1\) is close to 1 if the table indicates a strong row-column dependence and close to 0 if the numbers across each row are in the same proportions to each other as the column totals are to each other. Cramer’s coefficient can also be written as: \[
\sqrt \frac{T}{N(q-1)}
\]

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Method
Pearson’s coefficient of mean square contingency is also used.

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Approach
Given as:
\[
R_2 = \sqrt \frac{T}{N + T}
\] Since the maximum value of \(T = N(q-1)\), the maximum value of \(R_2\) is:
\[
R_2 (max)= \sqrt \frac{N(q-1)}{N + N(q-1)} = \sqrt \frac{q-1}{q}
\] which is close to 1 in most cases. The smallest value of \(T\) is 0, so:
\[
0 \leq R_2 \leq \sqrt\frac{q-1}{q} < 1.0
\]

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Method
Pearson’s mean-square contingency coefficient is also used as a measure of dependence.

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Approach
Given as:
\[
R_3 = \frac{T}{N}
\] for which this can be concluded from previous discussions:
\[
0 \leq R_3 \leq q-1
\] Note: knowledge of \(r\) and \(c\) is necessary in order to accurately interpret the degree of independence from the value of \(R_3\).

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Method
The Phi coefficient preserves direction. If the type of association is of interest, we must take care to set up the table in a way so that \(a\) and \(d\) represent the number of similar classifications, while \(b\) and \(c\) represent the number of unlike classifications.

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Approach
Given as:
\[
R_5 = \frac{ad-bc}{\sqrt{r_1 r_2 c_1 c_2}}
\] which may vary from +1, when all items are classified in the “alike” cells (both \(c\) and \(b\) equal zero), to -1, when all items are classified as “unlike” (both \(a\) and \(d\) equal zero). Phi coefficient is Cramer’s coefficient with the sign of \((ad-bc)\) being preserved. It is popular because it is a special case of the Pearson product moment correlation coefficient, computed by represented the classes as numbers.

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Hypotheses
One tailed test (only appropriate for 2x2 contingency table): Based on the phi coefficient of \[
R_5 = \frac{T_1}{\sqrt{N}}
\] where \(T_1\) is given by a previous equation 1 in section 4.1 and is approximately normally distributed. Therefore, \(\sqrt{N} * R_5\) is approximately normally distributed. - \(H_0\): There is no positive/negative correlation - \(H_A\): There is a positive/negative correlation

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Rejection Region
For positive correlation:

Reject \(H_0\) if \(\sqrt{N} * R_5\) exceeds \(z_{1-\alpha}\) from Table A1, with a level of \(\alpha\)

For negative correlation:

Reject \(H_0\) if \(\sqrt{N} * R_5\) smaller than \(z_{\alpha}\) from Table A1, with a level of \(\alpha\)

where t = a 1 x 4 vector or a 2 x 2 matrix, and digits = round the result to digits.

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Method
The Chi-Squared test for goodness-of-fit is designed to compare the sample obtained with the hypothesized distribution (chi-squared in this case) to see if the hypothesized distribution function fits the data in the sample. The data consists of \(N\) independent observations of a random variable \(X\). These \(N\) observations are grouped into \(c\) classes. The number of observations in each class are presented in the form of a 1xc contingency table.

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Assumptions

The sample is a random sample
The measurement scale is at least nominal

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
There are no direct parametric equivalents of the chi-squared goodness of fit test because it is used on categorical data and does not assume a particular distribution of the underlying variable. Parametric tests that are similar to the chi-squared test do exist for specific kinds of variables, such as the one-sample t test for continuous, categorically-grouped data.

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Hypotheses

\(H_0\): \(P(X\) is in class \(j = p_j^*\) for \(j=1, 2, ..., c\)
\(H_A\): \(P(X\) is in class \(j \neq p_j^*\) for at least one class

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Rejection Region

Reject \(H_0\) if \(T > 1-\alpha\) quantile of the chi-squared distribution with \(c-1\) degrees of freedom from Table A2.

title: Week 06: Chapter 4.4-4.5
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: Let \(p_j^*\) be the probability of a random observation on \(X\) being in class \(j\), under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true. Then

\[
E_j = p_j^*N
\] where \(j = 1, 2, ..., c\) and \(E_j\) represents the expected number of observations in class \(j\) when \(H_0\) is true. The test statistic \(T\) is given by: \[
T = \sum_{j=1}^c  \frac{(O_j - E_j)^2}{E_j}
\] OR \[
T = \sum_{j=1}^c  \frac{O_j^2}{E_j} - N
\]

The chi squared distribution with \(c-1\) degrees of freedom is used as an approximation since the exact distribution of \(T\) is difficult to use.
The p-value is approximately the probability of chi squared random variable with \(c-1\) degrees of freedom exceeding the observed value of \(T\) (obtained from Table A2).

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Method 1
The Chi-squared Test for difference in probabilities with a 2x2 contingency table is used to test if the probability of an event is the same for both populations that the random samples are drawn from.
A random sample of \(n_1\) observations is drawn from one population (or before a treatment is applied) and each observation is classified into either class 1 or 2, the total number of classes being \(O_{11}\) and \(O_{12}\), where \(O_{11} + O_{12} = n_1\). A second random sample of \(n_2\) observations is drawn from a second population (or the first population after some treatment is applied) and the number of observations in class 1 or class 2 is \(O_{21}\) and \(O_{22}\), where \(O_{21} + O_{22} = n_2\). This data can be arranged into a 2x2 contingency table with the total number of observations denoted as \(N\).

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Assumptions

Each sample is a random sample
The two samples are mutually independent
Each observation may be categorized either into class 1 or class 2

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
The book does not specifically mention a parametric equivalent. However, a quick search on Google allowed me to find the two-proportion Z-test, which seems to be fairly similar to the two-tailed version of this test. More information on this test can be found through this link: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-proportion_Z-test.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Hypotheses

\(H_0\): \(p_1 = p_2\) (two-tailed) | \(p_1 \geq p_2\) (left-tailed) | \(p_1 \leq p_2\) (right-tailed)
\(H_A\): \(p_1 \neq p_2\) (two-tailed) | \(p_1 < p_2\) (left-tailed) | \(p_1 > p_2\) (right-tailed)

where \(p_1\) is the probability that a randomly selected element will be in class 1 (in population 1) and \(p_2\) in population 2. Note: \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) do not have to be known explicitly.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Rejection Region
Two-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at the approximate level \(\alpha\) if \(T_1 <\) the \(\alpha/2\) quantile of a standard normal random variable \(Z\), or if \(T_1 > 1 - \alpha/2\) quantile of \(Z\) (\(Z\) is given in Table A1).

Left-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at the approximate level of \(\alpha\) if \(T_1 < \alpha\) quantile of \(Z\) found in Table A1.

Right-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at the approximate level of \(\alpha\) if \(T_1 > 1 - \alpha\) quantile of \(Z\) found in Table A1.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: If any column total is zero, \(T_1 = 0\). Otherwise: \[
T_1 = \frac {\sqrt{N}(O_{11}O_{22}-O_{12}O_{21})}{\sqrt{n_1 n_2 C_1 C_2}}
\] Note: for two-tailed hypotheses, \(T_1^2\) is often used over \(T_1\) as the test statistic. Then the rejection region is the upper tail of the chi-squared distribution with 1 degree of freedom (given in Table A2).
The null distribution of \(T_1\) is hard to calculate exactly due to all the different combinations of the contingency table. Thus, large sample approximation is used, which is the standard normal distribution (refer to Table A1).
The p-value is obtained differently for the different forms:

Two-tailed: p-value is twice the smaller of the probabilities that \(Z \leq\) or \(\geq\) the observed value of \(T_1\) (observed from Table A1)
Left-tailed: p-value is the probability that \(Z <\) observed value of \(T_1\)
Right-tailed: p-value is the probability that \(Z >\) observed value of \(T_1\)

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Method 2
Fisher’s Exact Test is also used with contingency tables, but only those with random row totals, random column totals, or both. The \(N\) observations in the data are summarized in a 2x2 contingency table usually. This is similar to the Chi-squared test for difference in probabilities, except both of the row totals, \(r\) and \(N-r\), and both column totals, \(c\) and \(N-c\), are predetermined/fixed.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Assumptions

Each observation is classified into exactly one cell.
The row and column totals are fixed, not random.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
Similarly to the Chi-squared test for differnce of probabilities, the book does not specifically mention a parametric equivalent. The two-proportion Z-test is fairly similar to the two-tailed version of this test. More information on this test can be found through this link: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-proportion_Z-test.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Hypotheses

\(H_0\): \(p_1 = p_2\) (two-tailed) | \(p_1 \geq p_2\) (left-tailed) | \(p_1 \leq p_2\) (right-tailed)
\(H_A\): \(p_1 \neq p_2\) (two-tailed) | \(p_1 < p_2\) (left-tailed) | \(p_1 > p_2\) (right-tailed)

where \(p_1\) is the probability of an observation in row 1 being classified into column 1, and \(p_2\) is the probability of an observation in row 2 being classified into column 1.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Rejection Region
Two-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at the level of significance \(\alpha\) if the p-value is \(\leq \alpha\).

Left-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at the level of significance \(\alpha\) if \(P(T_2 \leq t_{obs}) \leq \alpha\)

Right-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at the level of significance \(\alpha\) if \(P(T_2 \geq t_{obs}) \leq \alpha\)

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: \(T_2\) is the number of observations in the cell row 1, column 1.
The exact distribution of \(T_2\) when \(H_0\) is true is given by the hypergeometric distribution: \[
P(T_2 = x) =
\frac{\binom{r}{x} \binom{N-r}{c-x}}{\binom{N}{c}}
\quad x = 0, 1, \ldots, \min(r,c)
\] = 0 for all other values of x. For large sample approximation, use this equation, which is the standard normal distribution given in Table A1: \[
T_3 = \frac{x - \frac{rc}{N}}{\sqrt{\frac{rc(N-r)(N-c)}{N^2 (N-1)}}}
\]
Let \(t_{obs}\) be the observed value of \(T_2\). The p-value is obtained differently for the different forms:

Two-tailed: p-value is twice the smaller of \(P(T_2 \leq t_{obs})\) or \(P(T_2 \geq t_{obs})\)
Left-tailed: p-value is \(P(T_2 \leq t_{obs})\)
Right-tailed: p-value is \(P(T_2 \geq t_{obs})\)

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Method 3
The Mantel-Haenszel test is very similar to the Fisher’s Exact test for 2x2 contingency tables. The Mantel-Haenszel tests association between two binary variables while controlling for a third (stratification variable). A good example of this would be treatment vs. outcome, stratified by age group or study site. The data is summarized in several 2x2 contingency tables, each with nonrandom row and column totals. The number of tables is \(k \geq 2\), and the \(i\)th table is represented with the following table:

library(gt)

df <- data.frame(
  Row = c("Row 1", "Row 2", "Col Total"),
  `Col 1` = c("`$x_{i}$`", "`$c_{i} - x_{i}$`", "`$c_{i}$`"),
  `Col 2` = c("`$r_{i} - x_{i}$`", "`$N_{i} - r_{i} - c_{i} + x_{i}$`", "`$N_{i} - c_{i}$`"),
  `Row Total` = c("`$r_{i}$`", "`$N_{i} - r_{i}$`", "`$N_{i}$`")
)

df %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything())

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Assumptions
These are the same assumptions as the Fisher’s exact test: 1. Each observation is classified into exactly one cell. 2. The row and column totals are fixed, not random.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
The parametric equivalent is a logistic regression with stratum fixed effects.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Hypotheses
Two-tailed:

\(H_0\): \(p_{1i} = p_{2i}\) for all \(i = 1, ..., k\)
\(H_A\): Either \(p_{1i} > p_{2i}\) for some \(i\), or \(p_{1i} < p_{2i}\) for some \(i\), but not both

Left-tailed:

\(H_0\): \(p_{1i} \geq p_{2i}\) for all \(i = 1, ..., k\)
\(H_A\): \(p_{1i} \leq p_{2i}\) for all \(i\), and \(p_{1i} < p_{2i}\) for some \(i\)

Right-tailed:

\(H_0\): \(p_{1i} \leq p_{2i}\) for all \(i = 1, ..., k\)
\(H_A\): \(p_{1i} \geq p_{2i}\) for all \(i\), and \(p_{1i} > p_{2i}\) for some \(i\)

where \(p_{1i}\) is the probability of an observation in row 1 being classified into column 1 in the \(i\)th contingency table, and \(p_{2i}\) is the probability of an observation in row 2 being classified into column 1 in the \(i\)th contingency table.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Rejection Region
Two-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at the level of significance \(\alpha\) if \(T_4\) exceeds \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) or if \(T_4 < z_{\alpha/2}\), where \(z_p\) represents the \(p\)th quantile of the standard normal distribution (Table A1).

Left-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha\) if \(T_4 < z_\alpha\) from Table A1.

Right-tailed:

Reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha\) if \(T_4 > z_{1-\alpha}\) from Table A1.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: \[
T_4 = \frac{\sum x_i - \sum \frac{r_i c_i}{N_i}}
{\sqrt{\sum \frac{r_i c_i(N_i -r_i)(N_i-c_i)}
{N_i^2 (N_i-1)}}}
\]
The null distribution of \(T_4\) when \(H_0\) is true is given by the standard normal distribution given in Table A1. Note: exact probabilities are improved by using a continuity correction (for left-tailed: add 0.5 to numerator of \(T_4\) before looking up the p-value in Table A1, for right-tailed subtract 0.5 from numerator before looking up p-value).
The p-value is obtained differently for the different forms:

Two-tailed: p-value is twice the probability of a standard normal random variable being < or > observed value of \(T_4\) (whichever is smaller)
Left-tailed: p-value is the probability of a standard normal random variable < observed value of \(T_4\)
Right-tailed: p-value is the probability of a standard normal random variable > observed value of \(T_4\)

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Completed Homework Problem

One hundred men and 100 women were asked to try a new toothpaste and to state whether they liked or did not like the new taste. Thirty-two men and 26 women said they did not like the new taste. Does this indicate a difference in preferences between men and women in general?


# create the 2x2 contingency table
toothpaste <- matrix(c(32, 68, 26, 74), 
                     nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

# run chi-squared test
chisq.test(toothpaste, correct = FALSE)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  toothpaste
X-squared = 0.87421, df = 1, p-value = 0.3498


Hypotheses

\(H_0:\) \(p_1 = p_2\)
\(H_1:\) \(p_1 \neq p_2\)

where \(p_1\) is the probability that a randomly selected element will be present in population of men, and \(p_2\) is the same probability but for the population of women.
Test Statistic and p-Value

\(T_1 = 0.87421\)
\(p = 0.3498\)

Rejection Region

Reject \(H_0\) if \(p < \alpha\); \(\alpha=0.05\).

Conclusion/Interpretation

Fail to reject \(H_0\).
There is not sufficient evidence to suggest that there is a difference in preferences between men and women in general.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Method 1
We move onto the Chi-squared test for differences in probabilities involving rxc contingency tables in 4.2. There are \(r\) populations in all, and one random sample is drawn from each population. Let \(n_i\) represent the number of observations in the \(i\)th sample from the \(i\)th population for \(1 \leq i \leq r\). Each observation in each sample can be classified into one of \(c\) different categories.
Let \(O_{ij}\) be the number of observations from the \(i\)th sample that fall into category \(j\), so: \(n_i = O_{i1} + O_{i2} + ... + O_{ic}\) for all \(i\). The data is arranged in a contingency table where the total number of observations from all samples is \(N = n_1 + n_2+ ... + n_r\).

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Assumptions

Each sample is a random sample
The outcomes of the various samples are all mutually independent among samples
Each observation may be categorized into exactly one of the \(c\) categories/classes

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
The parametric equivalent is logistic regression (for binary outcomes) or multinomial logistic regression (for >2 outcome categories).

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Hypotheses
Let the probability of a randomly selected value from the \(i\)th population being classified in the \(j\)th class be denoted by \(p_{ij}\), for \(i = 1, 2, ..., r\) and \(j = 1, 2, ..., c\).

\(H_0\): All of the probabilities in the same column are equal to each other (i.e., \(p_{1j} = p-{2j} = ... = p_{rj}\), for all \(j\))
\(H_A\): At least two of the probabilities in the same column are not equal to each other (i.e., \(p_{ij} \neq p_{kj}\) for some pair \(i\) and \(k\))

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Rejection Region

The critical region of approximate size \(\alpha\) corresponds to values of \(T\) larger than \(x_{1-\alpha}\), the \(1-\alpha\) quantile of a chi-squared random variable with \((r-1)(c-1)\) degrees of freedom obtained from Table A2.
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T > x_{1-\alpha}\).

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: \[
T = \sum_{i = 1}^r  \sum_{j=1}^c   \frac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}
\] where \(E_{ij} = \frac {n_i C_j}{N}\).
The null distribution of \(T\) is approximately the chi-squared distribution with \((r-1)(c-1)\) degrees of freedom, whose quantiles are in Table A2.
The p-value is the probability of a chi-squared random variable with \((r-1)(c-1)\) degrees of freedom exceeding the observed value of \(T\), which can also be found in Table A2.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Method 2
The Chi-squared test for independence is performed to see whether or not the rows and columns of an rxc contingency table represent two independent classification schemes.
A random sample of size \(N\) is obtained. The observations can be classified according to two different criteria. Let \(O_{ij\) be the number of observations associated with row \(i\) and column \(j\) simultaneously. The total number of observations in row \(i\) is denoted as \(R_i\) and in column \(j\) by \(C_j\).

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Assumptions

The sample of \(N\) observations is a random sample. (Each observation has the same probability as every other observation of being classified in row \(i\) column \(j\), independently from the other observations)
Each observation may be classified into exactly one of \(r\) different categories according to one criterion and into exactly one of \(c\) different categories according to a second criterion.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
The parametric equivalent is log-linear models or logistic regression (in the 2×2 case).

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Hypotheses

\(H_0\): The event “an observation is in row \(i\)” is independent of the event “that same observation is in column \(j\)”, for all \(i\) and \(j\). AKA, P(row \(i\), column \(j\)) = P(row \(i\)) * P(column \(j\)), for all \(i\) and \(j\)
\(H_A\): P(row \(i\), column \(j\)) \(\neq\) P(row \(i\)) * P(column \(j\)), for some \(i\) and \(j\)

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Rejection Region

Reject \(H_0\) if \(T > x_{1-\alpha}\) quantile of a chi-squared random variable with \((r-1)(c-1)\) degrees of freedom (obtained from Table A2).

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: \[
T = \sum_{i = 1}^r  \sum_{j=1}^c   \frac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}
\] where \(E_{ij} = \frac {n_i C_j}{N}\). (Identical to previous method)
The null distribution of \(T\) is approximately the chi-squared distribution with \((r-1)(c-1)\) degrees of freedom, whose quantiles are in Table A2.
The p-value is the probability of a chi-squared random variable with \((r-1)(c-1)\) degrees of freedom exceeding the observed value of \(T\), which can also be found in Table A2.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
R function
R function for chi-squared test (obtained from https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/chisq.test)
chisq.test(x, y = NULL, correct = TRUE, p = rep(1/length(x), length(x)), rescale.p = FALSE, simulate.p.value = FALSE, B = 2000)

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Method 3
The Chi-squared test with fixed marginal totals is similar to the previous methods, except the row and column totals are determined beforehand, and therefore are fixed, not random.
The row and column totals are denoted by \(n_i\) and \(c_j\) to emphasize that they are not random. The total number of observations is \(N\).

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Assumptions

Each observation is classified into exactly one cell
The observations are on a random sample
The row and column totals are given, not random.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
There is not a parametric equivalent specifically listed because the fixed margins assumption is conditional. However, Fisher’s exact test’s underlying distribution, the hypergeometric distribution, is the exact parametric equivalent in this case. You could probably used conditional logistic regression when the margins are fixed by design.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Hypotheses
Let the probability of a randomly selected value from the \(i\)th population being classified in the \(j\)th class be denoted by \(p_{ij}\), for \(i = 1, 2, ..., r\) and \(j = 1, 2, ..., c\).

\(H_0\): All of the probabilities in the same column are equal to each other (i.e., \(p_{1j} = p-{2j} = ... = p_{rj}\), for all \(j\))
\(H_A\): At least two of the probabilities in the same column are not equal to each other (i.e., \(p_{ij} \neq p_{kj}\) for some pair \(i\) and \(k\))

OR

\(H_0\): The event “an observation is in row \(i\)” is independent of the event “that same observation is in column \(j\)”, for all \(i\) and \(j\). AKA, P(row \(i\), column \(j\)) = P(row \(i\)) * P(column \(j\)), for all \(i\) and \(j\)
\(H_A\): P(row \(i\), column \(j\)) \(\neq\) P(row \(i\)) * P(column \(j\)), for some \(i\) and \(j\)

(can be tailored to fit each problem)

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Rejection Region

The critical region of approximate size \(\alpha\) corresponds to values of \(T\) larger than \(x_{1-\alpha}\), the \(1-\alpha\) quantile of a chi-squared random variable with \((r-1)(c-1)\) degrees of freedom obtained from Table A2.
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T > x_{1-\alpha}\).

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: \[
T = \sum_{i = 1}^r  \sum_{j=1}^c   \frac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}
\] where \(E_{ij} = \frac {n_i C_j}{N}\). (same as other methods)
The null distribution of \(T\) is approximately the chi-squared distribution with \((r-1)(c-1)\) degrees of freedom, whose quantiles are in Table A2.
The p-value is the probability of a chi-squared random variable with \((r-1)(c-1)\) degrees of freedom exceeding the observed value of \(T\), which can also be found in Table A2.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
R function
R function for chi-squared test (obtained from https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/chisq.test)
chisq.test(x, y = NULL, correct = TRUE, p = rep(1/length(x), length(x)), rescale.p = FALSE, simulate.p.value = FALSE, B = 2000)

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Completed Homework Problem

In another study, all of the horses in all of the races for three days were classified by post position and by the order in which they finished. Is the horse’s position at the end of the race dependent on post position? Which test of this section is being used? (see code for contingency table)

I believe the fixed marginal totals chi-squared test should be applied to this problem.

horses <- matrix(c(15, 14, 15, 52, 9, 10, 9, 72), nrow = 2, ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE)
chisq.test(horses)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  horses
X-squared = 6.8137, df = 3, p-value = 0.07808


Hypotheses

\(H_0:\) Post position and finish position are independent.
\(H_1:\) Post position and finish position are not independent.

Test Statistic and p-Value

\(T_1 = 6.8137\)
\(p = 0.07808\)

Rejection Region

Reject \(H_0\) if \(p < \alpha\); \(\alpha=0.05\).

Conclusion/Interpretation

Fail to reject \(H_0\).
There is not sufficient evidence to suggest that the horse’s position at the end of the race dependent on post position.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Method
The Median Test examines whether several samples came from populations having the same median. It is basically a special application of the chi-squared test with fixed marginal totals.
From the \(c\) populations, a random sample size \(n_i\) where \(i = 1, 2,..., c\) is obtained. Then, the combined sample median, or grand median, is determined. Let \(O_{1i}\) be the number of observations in the \(i\)th sample that exceed grand median (AKA \(a\) in contingency table). Let \(O_{2i}\) be the number of observations in the \(i\)th sample that are \(\leq\) grand median (AKA \(b\) in contingency table). Arrange the frequency counts into a 2xc contingency table.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Assumptions

Each sample is a random sample.
The samples are independent of each other
The measurement scale is at least ordinal
If all populations have the same median, all populations have the same probability \(p\) of an observation exceeding the grand median

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
The parametric equivalents for the median test are the two-sample test (for comparing 2 medians/means) and one-way ANOVA (for comparing \(k\) medians/means).

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Hypotheses

\(H_0\): All \(c\) populations have the same medians
\(H_A\): At least two of the populations have different medians

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Rejection Region

Critical region of approximate size \(\alpha\) corresponds to values of \(T > x_{1-\alpha}\), the \(1-\alpha\) quantile of a chi-squared random variable with \((c-1)\) degrees of freedom obtained from Table A2.
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T > x_{1-\alpha}\).
Note: if \(H_0\) is rejected, pairwise multiple comparisons may be made between populations by using the median test repeatedly on 2x2 contingency tables. In each comparison, the median is found and the number above/below that median is used in the 2x2 contingency table. This does distrot the true level of significance of all tests but the first.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic (rearranged from previous section, note that \(O_{2i} = n_i - O_{1i}\) in the special case of two rows): \[
T = \frac {N^2}{ab} \sum_{i=1}^c  \frac{(O_{1i} - \frac{n_i a}{N})^2}{n_i}
\]
If \(a\) is approximately equal to \(b\), the following simplification can be used, and is exact if \(a=b\), approximate otherwise: \[
T = \sum_{i = 1}^c  \frac{(O_{1i}-O_{2i})^2}{n_i}
\]
The null distribution of \(T\) is approximately the chi-squared distribution with \((c-1)\) degrees of freedom. (difficult to tabulate the exact distribution of \(T\))
The p-value is approximately the probability of a chi-squared random variable with \((c-1)\) degrees of freedom exceeding the observed value of \(T\), which can be found in Table A2.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
R function
R function for median test (obtained from https://www.statology.org/moods-median-test-r/)
median_test(response~group, data)
where response is a vector of response values, group is a vector of grouping values, and data is a data frame containing the response and group vectors.

title: Week 05: Chapter 4.1-4.3
text:
Completed Homework Problem

A number of oil leases were auctioned to the highest bidder. Each lease received one or more selaed bids. Test the hypothesis that the leases that eventually became producers of oil have the same medium number of bids as the leases that never produced oil. A random sample of each type of lease is given below (see code for values).


library(coin)

Loading required package: survival

producers <- c(6, 3, 1, 14, 8, 9, 12, 1, 3, 2, 1, 7)   
nonproducers <- c(6, 2, 1, 1, 3, 1, 2, 4, 8, 1, 2) 

# put into a data frame
df <- data.frame(
  bids = c(producers, nonproducers),
  group = factor(c(rep("Producer", length(producers)),
                   rep("Nonproducer", length(nonproducers))))
)

median_test(bids ~ group, data = df, distribution = "exact")


    Exact Two-Sample Brown-Mood Median Test

data:  bids by group (Nonproducer, Producer)
Z = -1.0911, p-value = 0.4003
alternative hypothesis: true mu is not equal to 0


Hypotheses

\(H_0\): The two groups (producer and nonproducers) have the same median number of bids
\(H_A\): At least one of the groups has a different median number of bids

Test Statistic and p-Value

\(T = -1.0911\)
\(p = 0.4003\)

Rejection Region

Reject \(H_0\) if \(p < \alpha\); \(\alpha=0.05\).

Conclusion/Interpretation

Fail to reject \(H_0\).
There is not sufficient evidence to suggest that the leases that eventually became producers of oil have the same medium number of bids as the leases that never produced oil.

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Method
The binomial test is used when a sample contains the outcomes of \(n\) independent trials. Each outcome can either be present in “class 1” or “class 2”, but cannot be present in both.

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Assumptions
The \(n\) trials in the experiment must be independent. Each trial has a probability \(p\) which results in the outcome “class 1”, where \(p\) is the same for all \(n\) trials.

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
Since the binomial test assumes the data follows a binomial distribution, there is no parametric equivalent. The book states that the binomial test is often considered the most powerful test, and therefore it is claimed to be both parametric and nonparametric.

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Hypotheses

\(H_0\): \(p = p^*\) for two-tailed, \(p \geq p^*\) for left-tailed, \(p \leq p^*\) for right-tailed
\(H_A\): \(p \neq p^*\) for two tailed, \(p < p^*\) for left-tailed, \(p > p^*\) for right-tailed

where \(p^*\) is some specified probability and \(0 \leq p^* \leq 1\).

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Rejection Region
Two-tailed:

Using Table A3 (from back of book) - find the values for \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) such that: \[
P(Y \leq t_1) = \alpha_1
\] \[
P(Y \leq t_2) = 1 - \alpha_2
\] where \(Y\) is the binomial random variable with parameters \(p*\) and \(n\), \(\alpha_1\) is the size of the lower tail, and \(\alpha_2\) is the size of the upper tail.
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T \leq t_1\) or if \(T > t_2\).

Left-tailed:

Using Table A3 (from back of book) - find the value for \(t\) such that: \[
P(Y \leq t) = \alpha
\]
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T \leq t\).

Right-tailed:

Using Table A3 (from back of book) - find the value for \(t\) such that: \[
P(Y \leq t) = 1 - \alpha
\]
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T > t\).

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: \(T = O_1\), where \(T\) is the number of times the outcome is “class 1”, and \(O_1\) is the number of observations in “class 1”.
Null distribution is used. The null distribution of \(T\) is the binomial distribution with parameters \(p = p*\) and \(n=\) the sample size. Normal approximation is used for other values of \(n\) and \(p\) (i.e. \(n>20\) & select \(p\) values).
The p-value is obtained differently for the different forms:

Two-tailed: p-value is twice the smaller of the probabilities that \(Y \leq\) or \(\geq\) the observed value of \(T\)
Left-tailed: p-value is the probability that $Y $ observed value of \(T\)
Right-tailed: p-value is the probability that \(Y \geq\) observed value of \(T\)

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
R function
R function for binomial test (obtained from https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/binom.test):
binom.test(x, n, p = 0.5, alternative = c(“two.sided”, “less”, “greater”), conf.level = 0.95)
where \(x\) = number of successes, or a vector of length 2 giving the numbers of successes and failures, respectively; \(n\) = number of trials; and \(p\) = hypothesized probability of success. Alternative denotes whether the test is two-tailed, left-tailed, or right-tailed. Conf.level is the confidence level, usually 95%.

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text: Confidence Interval

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Data
A sample of observations on \(n\) independent trials is examined and the number \(Y\) of times the specified event occurs is noted.

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Assumptions

The \(n\) trials are mutually independent.
The probability \(p\) of the specified event occurring remains constant from one trial to the next.

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Approach
Approach A:

For \(n \leq 30\) and confidence coefficients of 0.90, 0.95, or 0.99, use Table A4.

Approach B:

For \(n > 30\) or confidence coefficients not covered in Table A4, use the normal approximation: \[
L = \frac{Y}{n} -z_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{Y(n-Y)/n^3}
\] and \[
U = \frac{Y}{n} +z_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{Y(n-Y)/n^3}
\]

where \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) is the quantile of a normally distributed random variable obtained from Table A1. The confidence coefficient is approximately \(1-\alpha\).

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Completed Homework Problem

It is known that 20% of a certain species of insect exhibit a particular characteristic A. Eighteen insects of that species are obtained from an unusual environment, and none of these have characteristic A. Is it reasonable to assume that insects from that environment have the same probability of 0.20 that the species in general has? Use a two-tailed test.


binom.test(0, 18, p = 0.2,
           alternative = c("two.sided"),
           conf.level = 0.95)


    Exact binomial test

data:  0 and 18
number of successes = 0, number of trials = 18, p-value = 0.03429
alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.2
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.000000 0.185302
sample estimates:
probability of success 
                     0 


Hypotheses

\(H_0:\) \(p = p^*\), where \(p^* = 0.20\)
\(H_1:\) \(p \ne p^*\)

Test Statistic and p-Value

\(T = 0\)
\(p = 0.03429\)

Rejection Region

Reject \(H_0\) if \(p < \alpha\); \(\alpha=0.05\).

Conclusion/Interpretation

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Method
The quantile test is a variation of the binomial test. It is used to test hypotheses that concern the quantiles of a random variable.

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Assumptions
The \(X_i\)s (i.e. \(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n\)) are a random sample (independent and identically distributed random variables). The measurement scale of the \(X_i\)s must be at least ordinal.

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
section: Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
text:
Parametric equivalent (or proof that there is none)
I obtained this information from these notes taken on this textbook: https://people.stat.sc.edu/hitchcock/notes518fall13sec32filledin.pdf
The quantile test about the median is testing the same thing as the t-test is about the mean. The quantile test is more efficient than the t-test when the population distribution is double exponential, or has heavy tails. Also, when considering the fact that the one sample t-test requires the data to be normal, the quantile test is more applicable and therefore preferred when it comes to nonparametric ordering statistics. However, the one sample t-test can be considered as the parametric equivalent to the nonparametric quantile test.

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Hypotheses

\(H_0\): The \(p^*\)th population quantile is \(x^*\) (two-tailed) | The \(p^*\)th population quantile is no greater than \(x*\) (left-tailed) | The \(p^*\)th population quantile is at least as great as \(x^*\) (right-tailed)
\(H_A\): \(x^*\) is not the The \(p^*\)th population quantile (two-tailed) | The \(p^*\) population quantile is greater than \(x^*\) (left-tailed) | The \(p^*\) population quantile is less than \(x^*\) (right-tailed)

In other words,

\(H_0\): \(P(X \leq x^*) \geq p^*\) and \(P(X < x^*) \leq p^*\) (two-tailed) | \(P(X \leq x^*) \geq p^*\) (left-tailed) | \(P(X < x^*) \leq p^*\) (right-tailed)
\(H_1\): \(P(X \leq x^*) < p^*\) (left-tailed) | \(P(X < x^*) > p^*\) (right-tailed) | (two-tailed is either or)

where \(x^*\) and \(p^*\) are some specified numbers and \(0 < p^* < 1\).

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Rejection Region
Two-tailed:

Using Table A3 (from back of book) - find the values for \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) such that: \[
P(Y \leq t_1) = \alpha_1
\] \[
P(Y \leq t_2) = 1 - \alpha_2
\] where \(Y\) has the binomial distribution with parameters \(p^*\) and \(n\), \(\alpha_1\) is the size of the lower tail, and \(\alpha_2\) is the size of the upper tail. The level of significance is \(\alpha_1 + \alpha_2\).
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T_1 \leq t_1\) or if \(T_2 > t_2\).

Left-tailed:

Using Table A3 (from back of book) - find the value for \(t_1\) such that: \[
P(Y \leq t_1) = \alpha
\]
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T_1 \leq t_1\).

Right-tailed:

Using Table A3 (from back of book) - find the value for \(t_2\) such that: \[
P(Y \leq t_2) = 1 - \alpha
\] OR \[
P(Y > t_2) = \alpha
\]
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T_2 > t_2\).

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Test Statistic and/or p-value

Test Statistic: \(T_1\) and \(T_2\), where \(T_1\) is the number of observations \(\leq x^*\) and \(T_2\) is the number of observations \(< x^*\). Then, \(T_1 = T_2\) if none of the numbers in the data set exactly equal \(x^*\); otherwise, \(T_1 > T_2\).
Null distribution is used. The null distribution of \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) is the binomial distribution with parameters \(p = p^*\) and \(n=\) the sample size. Normal approximation is used for other values of \(n\) and \(p\) (i.e. \(n>20\) & select \(p\) values).
The p-value is obtained differently for the different forms:

Two-tailed: p-value is twice the smaller of the probabilities that \(Y \leq\) or \(\geq\) the observed value of \(T_1\) or \(\geq\) the observed value of \(T_2\)
Left-tailed: p-value is the probability that \(Y \leq\) observed value of \(T_1\)
Right-tailed: p-value is the probability that \(Y \geq\) observed value of \(T_2\)

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text: Confidence Interval

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Data
The data consists of observations \(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n\) which are independent and identically distributed random variables. \(X^{(1)} \leq X^{(2)} \leq ... \leq X^{(r)} \leq ... \leq X^{(n)}\) represents the ordered sample, where \(1 \leq r < s \leq n\). We want to find the CI for an unknown \(p^*\)th quantile, where \(p^*\) is some specified number between 0 and 1.

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Assumptions

The sample \(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n\) is a random sample
The measurement scale of the \(X_i\)s is at least ordinal

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Approach
Approach A:

For \(n \leq 20\), Table A3 can be used to find \(s\) and \(r\). Specific instructions on finding \(s\) and \(r\) can be found on pg 143 of textbook.

Approach B:

For \(n > 20\), use the approximation based on the central limit theorem. Compute: \[
r^* = np^* -z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{np^*(1-p^*)}
\] and \[
s^* = np^* -z_{1-\alpha/2} \sqrt{np^*(1-p^*)}
\]

where \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) is obtained from Table A1. The confidence coefficient is approximately \(1-\alpha\).
One-sided confidence intervals are of the form: \[
P(X^{(r)} \leq x_{p^*}) = 1 - \alpha_1
\] and, if the distribution is continuous: \[
P(x_{p^*} \leq X^{(s)}) = 1 - \alpha_2
\] or, if not continous: \[
P(X^{(r)} \leq x_{p^*}) \geq 1 - \alpha_1
\] and \[
P(x_{p^*} \leq X^{(s)}) \geq 1 - \alpha_2
\]

title: Week 03: Chapter 3.1-3.2
text:
Completed Homework Problem
A good example for the quantile test is found here: https://people.stat.sc.edu/hitchcock/notes518fall13sec32filledin.pdf

The sergeant recalls that in the “good old days” the upper quartile for time required to complete the obstacle course was 42 minutes. He suspects that the new recruits are not as fit as the recruits in the good old days, so he times them on the obstacle course. He finds that out of 38 recruits, only ten of them complete the course within the 42 minute time period. Use the quantile test to test the hypothesis that the upper quartile is 42 minutes against the appropriate one-sided alternative.


#make a fake data set just to be able to use this function
x <- c(rep(42,10), rep(43,28))

quantile.test(x, xstar=42, quantile=0.75, alternative="quantile.greater")

$xstar
[1] 42

$alternative
[1] "quantile.greater"

$T1
[1] 10

$T2
[1] 0

$p.value
[1] 4.165498e-10


Hypotheses

\(H_0:\) \(P(X \leq x^*) \geq p^*\), where \(x^* = 42\) and \(p^* = 0.75\) for the upper quartile
\(H_1:\) \(P(X \leq x^*) < p^*\)

Test Statistic and p-Value

\(T_1 = 10\)
\(T_2 = 0\)
\(p = 4.165498e-10\)

Rejection Region

Reject \(H_0\) if \(p < \alpha\); \(\alpha=0.05\).

Conclusion/Interpretation

Reject \(H_0\).
There is sufficient evidence to suggest that the upper quartile of completion time for the obstacle course is greater than 42 minutes.
